passage: Emil had the highest mark in the class on the Cold War test, 94, and his father put the paper on the fridge in their Copenhagen flat. Emil had made flashcards only of the dates and names from the teacher's review sheet, drilled them until midnight, and skipped the chapter's extra pages completely. A week later, on the bus, Priscila was reading a novel about a family split by the Berlin Wall. "Why did they build the wall, anyway?" she asked. "You know this stuff." Emil opened his mouth. He remembered the answer had been on a flashcard. He couldn't remember what the card said. "It wasn't on the review sheet," he said, and looked out of the window.

qa.q: What mark did Emil get on the Cold War test?
qa.a: 94, the highest mark in the class.

qa.q: What might Emil have felt when he couldn't answer Priscila?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and a little uneasy, realising the 94 hadn't left him with anything he could explain.

qa.q: What could Emil try when studying the next chapter?
qa.a: He could read one of the extra pages that interests him and explain it to Priscila, so he learns something beyond the review sheet.

qa.q: How might Emil's father see the 94 if he had heard the bus conversation?
qa.a: He might still be proud, but he might also wonder whether the mark on the fridge shows real learning or just good drilling.

grounding: A teenager in Denmark crams only what will be tested, scores top marks, and cannot explain the topic a week later.

passage: At the coaching institute, Karthik's rank moved up to 12 on the weekly board, and his mother called to say she'd told the whole family. He had a system: only questions from the last ten years' papers, highlighted in three colours, memorised by pattern. When Sabina stayed back after class to ask the chemistry sir why ice floats, Karthik rolled his eyes. "That's not coming in the exam, Sabina. Waste of time." Two months later, the revision test covered a chapter from weeks before. Karthik sat staring at a question he was sure he had "done". Sabina, three rows ahead, was writing fast. Karthik's rank slipped to 31. On the bus he opened the old papers again, jaw tight, and started the highlighting all over.

qa.q: What rank did Karthik reach on the weekly board?
qa.a: His rank moved up to 12 on the weekly board.

qa.q: Why did Karthik think Sabina's question was a waste of time?
qa.a: He studies for rank and his mother's pride, so anything not coming in the exam feels useless to him.

qa.q: What could Karthik try instead of starting the highlighting all over?
qa.a: He could ask 'why' about a few topics, the way Sabina does, so the ideas stick longer than the next test.

qa.q: What might studying feel like for Sabina compared with Karthik?
qa.a: Sabina seems curious rather than pressured, so the chemistry stays interesting and is easier to remember weeks later.

grounding: A coaching student crams only exam patterns for rank and approval, and forgets them by the revision test.

passage:
Dear Vikas bhaiya,
Good news first: I came first in the Class 10 prelims! Papa distributed laddoos to the whole building. 98 in science. 😊
Now the weird part. You asked last month what I found most interesting in biology this year. I sat down to write back and... nothing. I don't remember any of it properly. I learned exactly what the question bank said, the night before each test, and it was gone the week after. Rank first, joy zero, if I'm honest.
Remember when we were small and you showed me frog eggs in the pond behind Nani's house? I asked a hundred questions. I don't ask anything now. There's no time, and there are no marks for it.
Is it like this in college too?
Sunaina

qa.q: What did Papa do when Sunaina came first?
qa.a: Papa distributed laddoos to the whole building.

qa.q: How does Sunaina seem to feel about coming first, beyond the good news?
qa.a: Sunaina feels a strange emptiness, 'rank first, joy zero', because the learning was only for tests and didn't stay.

qa.q: What small step could Sunaina take to bring back the questions?
qa.a: Sunaina could pick one biology topic, like the frog eggs, and explore it just out of curiosity, maybe writing to Vikas bhaiya about it.

qa.q: How might Vikas bhaiya feel reading that Sunaina doesn't ask anything now?
qa.a: He might feel sad, remembering the child with a hundred questions at the pond, and want to help Sunaina find that curiosity again.

grounding: A teenager writes that studying only for rank brought first place but left no memory or curiosity.

passage:
You want to know my secret, Sarita didi? There's no secret. I study exactly what comes in the exam. Last ten years' papers, the teacher's hints, highlight, mug up, done. Rank two in the class. Papa put the report card up at the shop and said, 'Vijay, rank one next time.'
What's photosynthesis? I knew it perfectly on the eighth of March. Ask me now... it's something with sunlight and... yeah, gone. Doesn't matter. It's not in the next exam.
What am I curious about? Uh. Nothing, really. I don't have time to be curious, didi. If it's not on the paper, why would I read it?
Sometimes Papa asks me things from the newspaper, about space or elections, and I have nothing to say. He looks a bit... never mind.
Anyway. Rank two. That's what counts, right?

qa.q: What does Vijay use to decide what to study?
qa.a: The last ten years' papers and the teacher's hints.

qa.q: Why does studying only for the exam feel sensible to Vijay?
qa.a: It delivers what Vijay values most, rank and Papa's pride; anything that isn't on the paper seems like wasted time.

qa.q: What moment could become a turning point for Vijay, and what choice could follow?
qa.a: When Papa asks about space or elections and Vijay has nothing to say; Vijay could pick one topic purely out of interest and read about it with no marks attached.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when Vijay has nothing to say about the newspaper questions?
qa.a: Papa seems a little disappointed: proud of the rank, but perhaps wishing Vijay were curious about the world as well.

grounding: A teenager crams only what will be tested for rank and a parent's approval, forgets it quickly, and has no curiosity left.

passage:
I'm Himani, Sarita's desk-mate in Class 9. Sarita is always in the top three, and her mother picks her up on result days with sweets.
Before the history test, Sarita made cards of only the questions Ma'am had hinted at. 'The rest won't come, why waste time?' She got 48 out of 50.
Two weeks later Ma'am asked about the same chapter for a new project. Sarita looked at her notebook, blank. Later she whispered to me, 'I've already deleted it from my head.'
Once I showed her a video on how the pyramids were built, and she asked, 'Is this in the syllabus?' I said no. She went back to her flash cards.
I don't know if she minds. She never seems bored. She never seems excited either.

qa.q: What score did Sarita get on the history test?
qa.a: 48 out of 50.

qa.q: What does Sarita's 'Is this in the syllabus?' suggest about what drives her?
qa.a: It suggests she values only what is tested and earns rank and her mother's sweets; interest for its own sake doesn't seem to count for her.

qa.q: What could Sarita choose to do to make learning last beyond the test?
qa.a: Sarita could explore one topic, like the pyramids video, with no marks attached, or explain a chapter to Himani after the test; using what is learnt keeps it and may spark curiosity.

qa.q: How does Himani see Sarita, compared with what her report card shows?
qa.a: The report card shows top-three ranks, but Himani sees someone who forgets fast and never seems excited, and can't tell whether Sarita minds.

grounding: A classmate observes a teenager who studies only hinted questions for rank, forgets them quickly and shows little curiosity.
